screens.title: Snapshot Backups and Filesystem-Level Approaches
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore filesystem-level snapshots as a fast and efficient approach for backing up MySQL data. Filesystem snapshots capture a point-in-time copy of the data directory almost instantly, which makes them ideal when recovery time and minimal disruption matter. We'll focus on Logical Volume Manager snapshots on Linux, the sequence to create a consistent snapshot for MySQL, and how to restore from a snapshot. You'll also learn about alternative snapshot technologies like ZFS, Btrfs, storage array snapshots, and cloud disk snapshots, and when snapshots are appropriate versus traditional logical or physical backups. Practically, we cover how to use the global read lock to ensure consistency, how copy-on-write snapshots work so snapshot creation is fast, how to mount and copy snapshot data, and how to merge a snapshot back to restore state. By the end you will understand the speed advantages, the storage and management trade-offs, and why combining snapshots with binary logs gives better point-in-time recovery. Think about an example: a busy OLTP server needs near-zero backup downtime — snapshots can meet that need if the data directory sits on a snapshot-capable volume. As you move through the lesson, notice the steps you would apply in your environment and one misconception to avoid: a snapshot alone is not the same as offsite backup.

screens.title: What is a Filesystem Snapshot?
screens.narratorSegment: A filesystem snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a volume or filesystem. In practice this means creating an addressable image that represents the state of files at a single instant. The most common implementation used in our Linux examples is copy-on-write. With copy-on-write, the snapshot does not duplicate all data at creation time; instead it records the original blocks and only stores copies of blocks when they are later changed. For MySQL this is powerful because creating the snapshot takes almost no time and keeps the database running with minimal interruption. For example, on a large InnoDB dataset you can acquire a short global read lock, trigger the snapshot, and then release the lock in seconds. A common misconception is that a snapshot is a complete offsite backup. It is not: a snapshot is local to the storage and must be copied elsewhere if you need offsite disaster recovery. Another misconception is that snapshots remove the need for binary logs. Snapshots capture full volume state at one moment; to recover to a specific transaction time between snapshots you still need binary logs. Key takeaway: snapshots give speed and low downtime, but plan for storage space, lifecycle management, and offsite copies.

keyIdea.title: Snapshot definition
keyIdea.text: A snapshot is a fast, point-in-time copy implemented with copy-on-write; it records changes after creation without duplicating all data immediately.

content.html:
Core Concept
Filesystem Snapshot
A point-in-time image of a volume that uses copy-on-write to remain fast and space-efficient.
Copy-on-write explained
  • At creation, snapshot references existing blocks — no bulk copy.
  • When origin writes to a block, the original block is copied to the snapshot area first.
  • This keeps snapshot creation instant while growth happens later.
Why it matters for MySQL

You can capture large datasets quickly, minimizing the period you hold a global read lock and reducing application downtime.

Key Takeaway

Snapshots are not replacements for offsite backups or binlog-based point-in-time recovery; they are a fast local copy that must be managed and exported.

Analogy

Think of a snapshot like a photographic negative of the filesystem taken instantly. As you keep taking new photographs, you only note differences rather than recreating the entire image.

Common misconception

A snapshot is not automatically offsite or multi-server. It captures a point-in-time image of a single volume and must be copied if you require offsite disaster recovery.

Concrete example

Acquire a brief global read lock on MySQL, create an LVM snapshot of the data LV, then release the lock and copy the mounted snapshot to your backup target.

screens.title: LVM Concepts: PV, VG, LV
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding LVM layout is essential before you use snapshots. LVM separates physical storage from logical volumes using three core layers: Physical Volumes, Volume Groups, and Logical Volumes. A physical volume is a disk or partition made available to LVM. Multiple physical volumes are combined into a volume group, which acts like a flexible pool of storage. Logical volumes are carved out of that pool and behave like block devices — these are where filesystems or MySQL data directories live. When you create an LVM snapshot you create a special logical volume that references an origin LV and records copy-on-write data. The architectural benefit is flexibility: you can grow, shrink, and snapshot LVs without changing partition tables. A common practical step is to verify the setup with commands that list volume groups and logical volumes. A misconception to watch for is assuming logical volumes map one-to-one to physical disks; they can span multiple physical devices, which influences performance and failure modes. Example: if /var/lib/mysql is on /dev/vg_mysql/lv_mysql_data you can snapshot that LV directly. Key takeaway: think of LVM as the storage abstraction layer that enables snapshots without stopping the filesystem.

keyIdea.title: LVM architecture
keyIdea.text: LVM provides a flexible storage layer: PVs -> VGs -> LVs; snapshots are special LVs that reference an origin volume and use copy-on-write.

content.html:
Definition
LVM Layers
Physical Volume (PV)
A disk or partition added to LVM's pool.
Volume Group (VG)
A storage pool combining one or more PVs.
Logical Volume (LV)
A block device carved from a VG for filesystems or applications.
Snapshot LV

A snapshot LV references an origin LV and stores changed blocks in a separate area using copy-on-write.

Verify your layout
Run the standard LVM listing commands to confirm that /var/lib/mysql is on an LV you can snapshot. If it is not on an LV, snapshots are not available without migration.
Concrete example

If your data LV is /dev/vg_mysql/lv_mysql_data you will create a snapshot LV referencing that origin. The snapshot consumes separate space for changed blocks while the origin continues serving IO.

screens.title: Preparing MySQL for a Consistent Snapshot
screens.narratorSegment: Before taking a filesystem snapshot you must ensure the database files are consistent on disk. For InnoDB and general MySQL data files the recommended command is to acquire a global read lock using the database's flush-and-lock mechanism. The standard pattern is to run a MySQL client command that issues FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK and keep that session open. That command flushes dirty pages to disk and prevents further writes, which guarantees the on-disk files reflect a coherent point-in-time. Important operational detail: do not close the session that holds the lock; closing it releases the lock and could make your snapshot inconsistent if the snapshot command required the lock. A common misconception is that stopping writes in the application is sufficient; without a flush-and-lock, in-memory changes or buffered writes might not be fully committed to disk. Example workflow: open a terminal, run a single client that calls flush-and-lock, keep it open. From a second terminal create the snapshot. When the snapshot command completes, return to the first session and unlock tables. Key takeaway: the global read lock window should be very short — usually seconds — so that the application impact is minimal, but it must be held while the snapshot creation command runs.

keyIdea.title: Consistency step
keyIdea.text: Use FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK and keep the session open while creating the snapshot to ensure on-disk consistency.

content.html:
Process Flow
Prepare MySQL
Acquire a global read lock to flush dirty pages and prevent writes before snapshot creation.
Step 1 — Acquire lock
Run the flush-and-lock command and keep that session open until the snapshot creation completes.
Step 2 — Create snapshot in separate terminal
Use your LVM snapshot command while the lock is still held, then immediately unlock.
Why keep the session open?

Closing the session releases the global read lock. If you close it before snapshot creation completes, the snapshot may capture an inconsistent mix of old and new writes.

Concrete example

Open Terminal A: run the flush-and-lock command and keep it open. Open Terminal B: run the lvcreate snapshot command. After lvcreate finishes, return to Terminal A and run unlock tables.

Common mistake

Do not run the lock and then close the session before creating the snapshot. Closing releases the lock and breaks consistency.

screens.title: Creating a Consistent LVM Snapshot — Step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk the full snapshot creation sequence. First, confirm your MySQL data directory is on an LVM logical volume. Use the standard LVM listing tools to identify the origin LV. Next, in one terminal acquire a global read lock by issuing the flush-and-lock command and keep that session open. From a separate terminal create the LVM snapshot with the lvcreate snapshot option. Pick a snapshot size large enough to capture changes while the snapshot exists; the practical guideline is roughly 10 to 20 percent of the origin size, adjusted for write activity. The snapshot creation itself is almost instantaneous because it only records metadata and sets up the copy-on-write area. As soon as lvcreate confirms the snapshot, release the lock in the MySQL session. After that, mount the snapshot to a temporary mount point and copy the files to your backup destination, or send them offsite. Finally, unmount and remove the snapshot to free space. A common operational tip: scripts should monitor snapshot space usage and remove old snapshots promptly so the copy-on-write area doesn't fill up. Example sequence demonstrates minimal downtime because the global read lock is held for only a few seconds, far shorter than a full physical file copy.

keyIdea.title: Practical sequence
keyIdea.text: Acquire lock, create lvcreate snapshot with adequate size, release lock, mount snapshot, copy data, then remove snapshot.

content.html:
Process Flow
Create an LVM Snapshot
Step A — Confirm LV location
Ensure /var/lib/mysql resides on an LV like /dev/vg_mysql/lv_mysql_data.
Step B — Acquire FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK
Keep this session open until snapshot creation completes.
Step C — Create snapshot
Use lvcreate -s with a snapshot name and size sized for write volume.
Step D — Release lock and copy snapshot data
Mount the snapshot and copy to your backup target, then remove the snapshot.
Sizing guideline

Start with roughly 10–20% of origin volume size as a snapshot allocation and adjust based on observed write activity during retention.

Operational tip

Automate cleanup and monitoring so snapshots do not accumulate or let the copy-on-write area fill, which would lead to failed snapshots or performance impact.

Concrete example

Create a 10G snapshot of /dev/vg_mysql/lv_mysql_data, mount it to /mnt/mysql_snapshot, copy files to your backup store, then unmount and lvremove the snapshot.

screens.title: Command Examples and Safe Practices
screens.narratorSegment: We'll review the canonical command patterns used when working with LVM snapshots. The safe pattern starts by running the flush-and-lock command in a MySQL client session. From a separate terminal you run the lvcreate snapshot command to create a snapshot LV referencing the origin. Choose a snapshot name that includes a timestamp to avoid collisions and pick a size sufficient for the expected writes while the snapshot exists. After creating the snapshot, you should immediately unlock tables in MySQL and then mount the snapshot volume to copy files. Once your backup is copied off the snapshot, unmount and remove the snapshot LV to release space. A common mistake is running lvcreate without holding the global read lock, which risks an inconsistent copy. Another pitfall is allocating too small a snapshot; if the copy-on-write area fills, the snapshot will fail. Example commands are often scripted in lab instructions, but remember: scripts must manage the lock lifespan and handle errors if the snapshot creation fails. Key takeaway: these commands are straightforward, but the sequence and monitoring are what guarantee a consistent and reliable backup.

keyIdea.title: Command pattern
keyIdea.text: Follow the lock, lvcreate, unlock, mount, copy, unmount, lvremove sequence and monitor snapshot space.

content.html:
Command Panel (illustrative)
# Terminal 1: hold lock
mysql -u root -p -e "FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK;" -- keep session open
# Terminal 2: create snapshot
sudo lvcreate -L 10G -s /dev/vg_mysql/lv_mysql_data -n mysql_data_snapshot_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS
# After lvcreate completes
mysql -u root -p -e "UNLOCK TABLES;"
# Mount snapshot and copy
sudo mount /dev/vg_mysql/mysql_data_snapshot_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS /mnt/mysql_snapshot
Safe practices
  • Keep the lock session open until lvcreate confirms.
  • Pick snapshot names with timestamps and remove them when done.
  • Monitor snapshot LV usage; avoid letting it fill.
Common mistake

Assuming snapshot creation copies files immediately; it is metadata-fast but the copy-on-write area grows as writes occur.

screens.title: Mounting, Copying, and Snapshot Cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: After creating a snapshot, the usual next step is to mount the snapshot logical volume and copy its files to your backup destination. Mounting the snapshot makes the consistent point-in-time file set available without affecting the live database. Copy operations should read the snapshot mount point and transfer files to offsite storage, object storage, or another safe target. Once the copy is confirmed, unmount the snapshot and remove the LV using the appropriate removal command. Remember that leaving snapshots active consumes space and can hurt performance; remove them promptly unless you intentionally retain them. A practical tip is to script integrity checks on the copied files before removing the snapshot, so you don't discard the only consistent image. An important misconception to avoid: a mounted snapshot is not a live, writable origin. Treat the snapshot as read-only for backup purposes. Example: mount the snapshot to /mnt/mysql_snapshot, rsync the directory to a backup store, then unmount and lvremove the snapshot LV. Key takeaway: manage snapshot lifecycle — mount, copy, verify, unmount, remove — to keep storage healthy and backups reliable. Mounting, Copying, and Snapshot Cleanup means mount the snapshot, copy files off-host, verify, then unmount and remove to free snapshot space and prevent performance issues.. In practical terms, from snapshot volume to backup target, then safe removal. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Mount, Copy, Clean
Make a reliable copy from the mounted snapshot and remove the snapshot when finished to reclaim space and avoid performance impacts.
Mount the snapshot
Create /mnt/mysql_snapshot and mount the snapshot LV there for read access.
Copy with verification
Copy files using a reliable tool and run integrity checks before deleting the snapshot.
Unmount and remove
Unmount the snapshot and run lvremove to delete the snapshot LV and free space.
Concrete scenario

Mount at /mnt/mysql_snapshot, rsync the data directory to a network backup, verify file checksums, then unmount and remove the snapshot LV.

Warning

Do not treat the snapshot mount as a place to perform live writes or schema migrations — it represents a frozen point-in-time copy for backup or recovery.

screens.title: Restoring from an LVM Snapshot
screens.narratorSegment: Restoration from an LVM snapshot is a fast rollback operation. The common procedure begins by stopping the MySQL server to ensure no processes hold or modify files during the merge. Next, merge the snapshot into the origin logical volume using the merge operation; this reverts the origin to the snapshot's state and removes the snapshot volume. After the merge completes, start MySQL and verify databases and tables. A typical issue after merging can be file permission or ownership problems, which can prevent MySQL from starting. The practical remedy is to set the correct ownership and permissions on the data directory for the mysql user and group and then attempt to start the service again. A misconception is thinking merge automatically fixes permissions; it does not. Process Flow
Restore from Snapshot
Merging reverts the origin to the snapshot moment. Stop MySQL first, then run the merge, then restart and verify.
Step 1 — Stop MySQL
Ensure the server is stopped so files are not in use during merge.
Step 2 — Merge the snapshot
Run the merge operation to restore the origin LV to the snapshot state. The snapshot LV is removed automatically after merge.
Step 3 — Restart and verify
Start MySQL and run queries to confirm the expected records are present and no extra writes occurred after the snapshot.
Common restore issue

After merge MySQL may fail to start due to ownership or permission mismatches. Fix ownership to mysql:mysql and set directory permissions appropriately before starting.

screens.title: Other Filesystem Snapshot Technologies
screens.narratorSegment: LVM is common on Linux, but other snapshot-capable systems exist and have their own advantages. ZFS is both a filesystem and volume manager with built-in snapshot capabilities that are efficient and highly flexible, often used in high-performance storage. Btrfs is another Linux filesystem with integrated snapshot functionality and similar copy-on-write behavior. Enterprise storage arrays implement hardware-level snapshots which offload the work from the server, often providing the fastest snapshot creation and minimal server overhead. Cloud providers also offer block-level snapshots for managed disks that behave like storage snapshots. For MySQL you apply the same consistency rule regardless of technology: ensure the database is in a consistent state before triggering the snapshot. The key differences are operational: array and cloud snapshots may be managed through vendor APIs and can provide better off-host performance, while ZFS and Btrfs offer native on-host snapshot control. A misconception is assuming all snapshots are equal — their management, performance characteristics, and offsite capabilities differ. Example decision: choose hardware or cloud snapshots where you want minimal server C P U impact, and choose ZFS or Btrfs when you want tight on-host control and file-system-level features.

Comparison
ZFS & Btrfs vs Arrays & Cloud
ZFS / Btrfs
Native filesystem snapshots with copy-on-write semantics and fine control on host.
Storage array snapshots
Hardware-level snapshots that offload work and can be the fastest option in enterprise systems.
Cloud disk snapshots
Provider-managed block snapshots that are convenient for cloud-hosted MySQL instances.
Practical note

Regardless of storage technology, acquire database consistency before triggering a snapshot. The exact API or command varies by system but the principle stays the same.

Misconception check

Don’t assume cloud snapshots automatically provide offsite long-term retention. They still need lifecycle and export planning for disaster recovery.

Concrete decision example

If you need minimal server CPU impact, prefer array or cloud snapshots; if you want full filesystem features locally, prefer ZFS or Btrfs.

screens.title: Benefits and Limitations of Snapshot-Based Backups
screens.narratorSegment: Snapshot-based backups are attractive because they are nearly instantaneous to create and typically require only a very short period holding a global read lock for consistency. This makes them ideal when recovery objectives are tight and backup windows must be minimal. Snapshots also enable very fast restores by rolling back volumes, which can meet aggressive RTOs. However, snapshots have limitations you must manage: they are tied to the underlying storage technology, so your data directory must reside on an LVM, ZFS, Btrfs, or snapshot-capable array. Snapshots are primarily a single-server solution and do not inherently provide distributed backups for multi-server topologies. They are full-volume images at a point in time, so achieving fine-grained recovery down to a particular transaction requires combining snapshots with binary logs. Snapshots consume space and can degrade performance if too many are active or if copy-on-write space fills. They also are local by default; you must plan a process to copy snapshot contents offsite for disaster recovery. Key takeaway: snapshots are powerful for speed and simplicity, but pair them with logs and offsite copies to form a complete recovery plan.

Comparison
Benefits vs Limitations
Benefits
  • Speed: almost instantaneous snapshot creation.
  • Minimal downtime: short lock window for consistency.
  • Fast restores: merge or rollback to snapshot state quickly.
Limitations
  • Dependent on storage technology and single-server focus.
  • Snapshots consume space and need lifecycle management.
  • Combine with binary logs for fine-grained point-in-time recovery.
Operational reminder

Plan snapshot sizing, monitoring, and offsite copying as part of any snapshot-based backup strategy to avoid surprises.

Key Takeaway

Use snapshots for speed, but pair with binary logs and an offsite copy to enable full disaster recovery and fine-grained restores.

screens.title: Hands-on: Perform and Restore an LVM Snapshot
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a test database, taking a consistent LVM snapshot, simulating data loss, and restoring from the snapshot. First, ensure your MySQL data directory is on an LVM logical volume. Create a test database and insert a row to record the initial state. Acquire the global read lock from Terminal A and, while holding it, create a snapshot with lvcreate from Terminal B. Release the lock and add more rows to simulate ongoing activity. To simulate data loss, drop the table or delete rows. Then stop MySQL and merge the snapshot back into the origin volume. Start MySQL and verify that only the initial record from before the snapshot remains. A common mistake is forgetting to verify snapshot existence before releasing the lock; always confirm the snapshot is present with LVM listing tools before unlocking. Filesystem snapshots capture a point-in-time copy of the data directory almost instantly, which makes them ideal when recovery time and minimal disruption matter. We'll focus on Logical Volume Manager snapshots on Linux, the sequence to create a consistent snapshot for MySQL, and how to restore from a snapshot. You'll also learn about alternative snapshot technologies like ZFS, Btrfs, storage array snapshots, and cloud disk snapshots, and when snapshots are appropriate versus traditional logical or physical backups. Practically, we cover how to use the global read lock to ensure consistency, how copy-on-write snapshots work so snapshot creation is fast, how to mount and copy snapshot data, and how to merge a snapshot back to restore state. By the end you will understand the speed advantages, the storage and management trade-offs, and why combining snapshots with binary logs gives better point-in-time recovery. Think about an example: a busy OLTP server needs near-zero backup downtime — snapshots can meet that need if the data directory sits on a snapshot-capable volume. As you move through the lesson, notice the steps you would apply in your environment and one misconception to avoid: a snapshot alone is not the same as offsite backup.

These objectives guide your practical mastery of snapshot backups for MySQL. First, you will understand what a filesystem snapshot is and why it is useful for quick, point-in-time copies. Second, you'll be able to explain how Logical Volume Manager snapshots operate using a copy-on-write model and why that model enables near-instant snapshot creation. Third, you'll be able to perform the standard, consistent LVM snapshot sequence for a MySQL data volume, including acquiring the global read lock and creating the snapshot without closing the lock prematurely. Fourth, you'll know how to restore from a snapshot using merge procedures and how to combine snapshots with binary logs for precise point-in-time recovery. Each objective includes a practical mnemonic so you can remember the steps under pressure, and a verified competency milestone you can use to mark proficiency once you've completed the hands-on activity.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on abilities and when to choose snapshots. You'll learn to size a snapshot volume, estimate the copy-on-write space needed using the 10 to 20 percent guideline, and monitor snapshot growth. You'll recognize the environments where snapshots are strong: virtualized servers, Linux hosts using LVM, and storage arrays with hardware snapshot features. You'll also learn to evaluate the limitations — single-server focus, snapshot management overhead, and the need to copy data offsite. These skills prepare you to decide whether snapshots alone meet your disaster-recovery needs or if you must combine them with logical backups and binary logs for fine-grained recovery. A small visual mnemonic compares local snapshot versus offsite backup so you remember to copy snapshot data off the server for true disaster recovery. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A filesystem snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a volume or filesystem. In practice this means creating an addressable image that represents the state of files at a single instant. The most common implementation used in our Linux examples is copy-on-write. With copy-on-write, the snapshot does not duplicate all data at creation time; instead it records the original blocks and only stores copies of blocks when they are later changed. For MySQL this is powerful because creating the snapshot takes almost no time and keeps the database running with minimal interruption. For example, on a large InnoDB dataset you can acquire a short global read lock, trigger the snapshot, and then release the lock in seconds. A common misconception is that a snapshot is a complete offsite backup. It is not: a snapshot is local to the storage and must be copied elsewhere if you need offsite disaster recovery. Another misconception is that snapshots remove the need for binary logs. Snapshots capture full volume state at one moment; to recover to a specific transaction time between snapshots you still need binary logs. Key takeaway: snapshots give speed and low downtime, but plan for storage space, lifecycle management, and offsite copies.

Understanding LVM layout is essential before you use snapshots. LVM separates physical storage from logical volumes using three core layers: Physical Volumes, Volume Groups, and Logical Volumes. A physical volume is a disk or partition made available to LVM. Multiple physical volumes are combined into a volume group, which acts like a flexible pool of storage. Logical volumes are carved out of that pool and behave like block devices — these are where filesystems or MySQL data directories live. When you create an LVM snapshot you create a special logical volume that references an origin LV and records copy-on-write data. The architectural benefit is flexibility: you can grow, shrink, and snapshot LVs without changing partition tables. A common practical step is to verify the setup with commands that list volume groups and logical volumes. A misconception to watch for is assuming logical volumes map one-to-one to physical disks; they can span multiple physical devices, which influences performance and failure modes. Example: if /var/lib/mysql is on /dev/vg_mysql/lv_mysql_data you can snapshot that LV directly. Key takeaway: think of LVM as the storage abstraction layer that enables snapshots without stopping the filesystem.

Before taking a filesystem snapshot you must ensure the database files are consistent on disk. For InnoDB and general MySQL data files the recommended command is to acquire a global read lock using the database's flush-and-lock mechanism. The standard pattern is to run a MySQL client command that issues FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK and keep that session open. That command flushes dirty pages to disk and prevents further writes, which guarantees the on-disk files reflect a coherent point-in-time. Important operational detail: do not close the session that holds the lock; closing it releases the lock and could make your snapshot inconsistent if the snapshot command required the lock. A common misconception is that stopping writes in the application is sufficient; without a flush-and-lock, in-memory changes or buffered writes might not be fully committed to disk. Example workflow: open a terminal, run a single client that calls flush-and-lock, keep it open. From a second terminal create the snapshot. When the snapshot command completes, return to the first session and unlock tables. Key takeaway: the global read lock window should be very short — usually seconds — so that the application impact is minimal, but it must be held while the snapshot creation command runs.

Next, in one terminal acquire a global read lock by issuing the flush-and-lock command and keep that session open. From a separate terminal create the LVM snapshot with the lvcreate snapshot option. Pick a snapshot size large enough to capture changes while the snapshot exists; the practical guideline is roughly 10 to 20 percent of the origin size, adjusted for write activity. The snapshot creation itself is almost instantaneous because it only records metadata and sets up the copy-on-write area. As soon as lvcreate confirms the snapshot, release the lock in the MySQL session. After that, mount the snapshot to a temporary mount point and copy the files to your backup destination, or send them offsite. Finally, unmount and remove the snapshot to free space. A common operational tip: scripts should monitor snapshot space usage and remove old snapshots promptly so the copy-on-write area doesn't fill up. Example sequence demonstrates minimal downtime because the global read lock is held for only a few seconds, far shorter than a full physical file copy.

From a separate terminal you run the lvcreate snapshot command to create a snapshot LV referencing the origin. Choose a snapshot name that includes a timestamp to avoid collisions and pick a size sufficient for the expected writes while the snapshot exists. After creating the snapshot, you should immediately unlock tables in MySQL and then mount the snapshot volume to copy files. Once your backup is copied off the snapshot, unmount and remove the snapshot LV to release space. A common mistake is running lvcreate without holding the global read lock, which risks an inconsistent copy.
